title: Aural Architecture as Affect: Understanding the Impact of Acoustic Environments on Human Experience
research_question: How does an acoustic environment influence human experience and impact emotions? What are the acoustic characteristics and parameters related to that emotional impact? What are the links between the acoustic characteristics and the emotional impact?

participants.description: 9 males and 11 females, aged 20-40 years old, from diverse cultural backgrounds (religious affiliation, nationalities).
participants.recruitment: Not explicitly stated, but implies volunteers for an experimental study.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Eight virtual reality scenes, each combining 360-degree visuals and 3D binaural audio. Four religious buildings (two mosques: Islamic Center of America (A1), Islamic Center of Detroit (A2); two churches: New Bethel Baptist Church (B1), Breakers Covenant Church International (B2)) were used. For each building, participants experienced a 'dry' recording (anechoic sound source) and a 'wet' recording (binaural recording of the sound source played in the actual building). Sound sources were Quran recitations for mosques and Christian hymns for churches. Visuals were identical for dry and wet recordings of the same building.

findings.antecedent: Room modes (multiple convolutions method)

findings.quote: Those peaks and dips become more distinguishable when the convolution is repeated multiple times (Fig. 3.6; right).

findings.antecedent: Building A1 (Islamic Center of America) reinforcing low and mid frequencies (120-800 Hz)
findings.mechanism: Reinforcement of dominant low and mid frequencies by the acoustic environment enhances spiritual emotional impact.
findings.quote: A1 was rated significantly higher for the emotional impact (spiritual) than A2 (Fig. 4.25), the results provide additional support to the link between spiritual emotions and acoustic environments that reinforces low and mid frequencies.

findings.antecedent: Auralization algorithm for low frequencies (<200 Hz)
findings.mechanism: Current auralization software may not accurately represent low frequencies, impacting subjective evaluation.
findings.quote: auralization results show a significant drop in the magnitude value at frequencies <200 Hz. This can be seen when comparing the spectra of the first auralization in Fig. 4.32and the wet recording (recorded in the building) in Fig. 4.34.

findings.antecedent: Acoustic environment (real space vs. artificial reverberation)
findings.mechanism: Natural reverberation in real spaces produces nonuniform amplification, unlike constant resonance densities in many artificial reverberators.
findings.quote: resonances that resulted from the sound reflections in a real space (Building A1) are more nonuniform than the ones generated by artificial reverberation, especially at low frequencies.

findings.antecedent: Acoustic environment (wet recording in A1, 2 channels)
findings.consequent: Magnitude difference at frequencies lower than 250 Hz
findings.mechanism: Directionality of sound reflections, especially at low frequencies, significantly impacts loudness perception.
findings.quote: magnitude difference >10 dB at frequencies lower than 250 Hz in A1 (using two channels of the ambisonic microphone). This difference is above the just-noticeable difference (JND)

findings.antecedent: Building with highest Bass Ratio (BR) and lower resonance width
findings.mechanism: Specific acoustic characteristics (high BR, low resonance width) are linked to higher emotional impact.
findings.quote: buildings with the highest BR and lower resonance width received a higher rating for emotional impact.

findings.antecedent: Building with higher resonance quality
findings.mechanism: Resonance quality is inversely related to resonance width, so higher quality implies higher emotional impact.
findings.quote: resonance width is inversely related to resonance quality, this also indicates that the buildings with higher resonance quality resulted in higher emotional impact.

mechanisms: The integration between the physical, perceptual, and cultural aspects of acoustics shapes the aural environment and impacts human experience.
Architectural features (geometry, materials) create specific acoustic characteristics (reverberation, resonance, amplification of frequency bands) that influence sound perception.
Sound characteristics (e.g., low frequencies, reverberation time, bass gain) directly evoke or enhance emotional responses (spiritual, calming, arousal).
Cultural background and familiarity with sound content or acoustic environments modulate the intensity of emotional impact, acting as priors in perception.
Mismatch or congruence between visual and aural cues affects comfort and perceived realism.
Room modes, identified through iterative auralization, selectively amplify or dampen frequencies, contributing to sound coloration and emotional effects.
Physiological responses (HRR, EDR) indicate emotional arousal, which can be linked to specific acoustic parameters and subjective emotional reports.
moderators: Cultural background (familiarity with recording content, familiarity with worship space)
Sound source characteristics (dominant frequencies, type of music/chant)
Listener's previous experience of sound events and environments
implementation_implications: Architects should consider aural aspects in design, especially for spaces where sound is integral to activities (e.g., worship, performance, meditative spaces, museums).
Design guidelines should be developed based on acoustic requirements that support specific emotional experiences, moving beyond mere noise reduction.

The developed auralization method can be used as a diagnostic tool to evaluate existing rooms and inform design decisions for modifying geometry, volume, and materials to achieve desired acoustic amplification across frequency bands.
Future research should explore architectural features that reinforce low frequencies to enhance spiritual emotions and investigate other frequency bands for different emotions.
Multisensory VR representations of cultural heritage can be designed using visual and aural documentation methods to enhance immersive experiences.
Auralization technology needs further development for more realistic representation of low frequencies to improve subjective evaluation in virtual acoustic environments.

limitations: Some results are specific to worship spaces and may not generalize to other building types; further studies are needed to examine different frequency bands for other kinds of emotions.
The study used binaural recording which did not account for head movement, potentially limiting the realism of the auditory experience.
Auralization in simulations can only estimate general bands where room modes occur and may not provide a realistic representation of low frequencies (<200 Hz).
